name: Isabella Color
lede: Isabella Color is a dark, greyish yellow-tan, a swatch from Ridgway's atlases of 1886 and 1912.

sections.title: The tan, not the near-white
sections.body:
The name is attached to a legend about an unwashed-linen vow, which the books read treat as doubtful, not as established [1][2]. St Clair notes that two dresses in the color appear in Queen Elizabeth I's wardrobe inventories, one taken a year before the siege the story is built around [1]. Paterson defines isabel as a dingy yellow-grey and records two possible Isabellas as suggestions only [2].

This swatch is Ridgway's, carried from his 1886 *Nomenclature of Colors* into the 1912 atlas (plate XXX) and the 1955 ISCC-NBS system, which calls it dark grayish yellow [3]. It is far darker than the near-white web [[white]] [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: It is one of the most frequent colors in museum painting: 4,445 of 23,781 paintings contain it, 18.7 per cent, more than 98 per cent of named colors [4]. It is most often an accent, and peaks in the 1300s, in 21.1 per cent of paintings [4]. Maarten van Heemskerck uses it in 7 of 12 works [4]. It shares canvases with [[dresden-brown]] and sits near [[tan]] [4]. Much of this tan is the yellowing of aged varnish [4].
